nameStory: The speckled swimming crab gets its name from two distinctive features that make it stand out in New England waters. Its shell is covered with tiny dark spots or speckles that look like someone flicked paint across its carapace. Unlike many crabs that scuttle along the bottom, this species is a skilled swimmer, using its flattened paddle-like back legs to glide gracefully through the water column.
description: The speckled swimming crab is a medium-sized marine crab with a distinctive spotted shell that makes it one of the more recognizable crabs in New England waters. Its carapace (shell) is typically brownish or grayish with numerous small dark speckles scattered across the surface. Like other swimming crabs, it has flattened rear legs that work like paddles, allowing it to swim rather than just walk along the seafloor. Adult speckled swimming crabs usually reach 3-4 inches across their shell.

idTips.label: Speckled Shell Pattern
idTips.description: The carapace has a distinctive pattern of small, dark spots scattered across a lighter brown or gray background, giving it a freckled appearance that's visible even underwater

idTips.label: Paddle-shaped Back Legs
idTips.description: The last pair of legs are flattened into oval paddles that feel smooth and blade-like, unlike the pointed claws and walking legs

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: The carapace is wider than it is long with a smooth, slightly domed surface that feels hard and glossy when touched

idTips.label: Sharp Side Spines
idTips.description: Five to six pointed spines project from each side of the shell, feeling sharp to the touch and giving the crab a somewhat aggressive appearance

idTips.label: Swimming Behavior
idTips.description: Often seen swimming in short bursts through the water rather than just scuttling on the bottom, moving with quick paddle strokes

habitat: Speckled swimming crabs prefer sandy and muddy bottoms in shallow coastal waters, typically found in depths from just below the low tide line to about 30 feet deep. They're most common in protected bays, harbors, and estuaries along the New England coast where they can easily bury themselves in soft sediment. You might spot them swimming near eelgrass beds or over sandy flats, especially during warmer months.

seasonality.spring: Crabs begin moving into shallower waters as temperatures warm, becoming more active and visible to observers in tide pools and shallow bays.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when speckled swimming crabs are most commonly seen swimming and foraging in shallow coastal waters, making this the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Crabs remain active but begin moving to slightly deeper waters as temperatures cool, though they can still be found in protected shallow areas.
seasonality.winter: Much less active and typically found buried in sediment in deeper waters, rarely observed by casual beachcombers during this season.

funFact: Speckled swimming crabs are accomplished underwater acrobats that can swim backwards, sideways, and even upside down by rapidly beating their paddle-shaped legs up to 20 times per second—making them some of the most agile swimmers in the crab world!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with blue crabs, but speckled swimming crabs have their distinctive spotted pattern while blue crabs are more uniformly colored. Remember: "Speckled has spots, blue crabs do not." The paddle-shaped back legs are similar in both species, so focus on the shell pattern for positive identification.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "swimming" crabs, these animals still spend much of their time on the seafloor and are excellent burrowers, able to quickly dig backwards into sand when threatened. The family name Portunidae comes from Portunus, the Roman god of harbors and ports, reflecting these crabs' preference for coastal waters.
compareHints: Since this is the only Arenaeus species in New England waters, compare it with other swimming crabs in the family Portunidae like the blue crab. Speckled swimming crabs are distinguished by their obvious spotted pattern and slightly smaller size compared to blue crabs. Unlike lady crabs which also have spots, speckled swimming crabs have much more pronounced paddle-shaped rear legs and a less rounded shell shape.
